questions.q: Per this lesson, why is a concentrated-liquidity LP position (from Lesson 9) commonly minted as an NFT rather than a fungible token?
options: Each position has a different price range, fee tier, and liquidity amount, making every position genuinely unique
NFTs are always cheaper to mint than ERC-20 tokens
Fungible tokens cannot represent any kind of financial position
It's purely a marketing choice with no functional reason
questions.explain: Because each concentrated-liquidity position's parameters differ, the NFT is the on-chain proof of that specific, non-interchangeable position.

questions.q: In the fractionalization example, an NFT with an implied value of $500,000 is split into 1,000,000 shares. What is the price per share?
Why do NFT-backed lending protocols typically use a lower loan-to-value ratio than fungible-asset lending protocols, per this lesson?
options: NFTs are always worth more than fungible tokens
A single NFT's value depends on floor price estimates, rarity traits, and thin order books -- harder to price than a liquid fungible token
Regulations ban NFT-backed loans from using high LTV
There is no real difference -- both use identical LTV ratios
questions.explain: Pricing a specific, illiquid NFT is harder than pricing a continuously-traded fungible asset, so protocols compensate with a lower LTV.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a "utility NFT" used with no trading intent, per this lesson?
options: An NFT fractionalized into ERC-20 shares for trading
An NFT used purely as loan collateral
An NFT representing a concentrated-liquidity LP position
An NFT that unlocks a Discord role or website feature, checked via balanceOf or ownerOf
questions.explain: Gated access (unlocking a role or feature by holding a specific NFT) is a functional-key use case with no trading intent, unlike fractionalization or collateral.

questions.q: If a borrower deposits an NFT worth an estimated $20,000 and the protocol offers 40% LTV, how much can they borrow?
questions.explain: Loan amount = collateral value x LTV = 20,000 x 0.40 = $8,000.
